# ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance

# ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Structure and components

- [statement] Repository retrieval needs maintained structure as well as storage: the ResearchOps Community includes taxonomies, structured vocabularies, librarianship and delivery of insights to research consumers; NN/g recommends a documented initial taxonomy that stays simple and evolves through use. (medium confidence) — https://researchops.community/blog/project/research-repositories/ · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/

## How it works

- [statement] Burghardt recommends checking current applicability through stakeholder flags, researcher review during reuse, or targeted review of a research subset. He also cautions against discarding research solely because it is old; age and present relevance require separate judgment. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends fully anonymised research extracts whenever possible and removing or obscuring direct identifiers, contact details and confidential information even when full anonymisation would remove useful context. Non-anonymised outputs require restricted sharing. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy
- [statement] Jake Burghardt proposes assessing evidence durability using collection or reporting date, research type, investigated topic, audience or market changes, and severity or priority. His example expiration rules are explicitly possibilities to adapt, not universal best practices; old research can remain applicable when its context has not changed. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] Research-data retention and insight relevance require separate judgments: GOV.UK says to establish a deletion process for unneeded data or expired retention and data without clear consent, while Burghardt describes research that satisfies governance rules but is no longer applicable to the product. Retaining data does not establish its relevance. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use citations from planning and decision artifacts back to research, and record reuse requests and their resulting work products. These practitioner practices make research use more traceable, but citation alone does not establish that a decision was correct or that research caused a business outcome. (medium confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] A research repository is distinguished by its research contents and purpose of consumption and reuse, rather than by a particular software category: the ResearchOps Community includes knowledge bases, wikis, drives and file cabinets, while UX Mastery describes searchable, reusable UX research data. (medium confidence) — https://github.com/researchops/research_repositories · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/
- [statement] For evidence traceability, Zack Naylor recommends insight records containing a name, contextual description, tags and supporting notes, observations, artifacts or data. Jake Burghardt recommends insight summaries that preserve study context and link to component reports and evidence; these are practitioner patterns rather than demonstrated universal requirements. (medium confidence) — https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/ · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions, https://skimle.com/blog/building-a-research-repository-that-people-actually-use
- [statement] Repository governance must accommodate deletion rather than indefinite evidence preservation: the Service Manual requires a deletion process for data no longer needed or at the end of retention, and organisation that permits finding and deleting a participant’s specific data. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy
- [statement] NN/g reports that missing ownership and burdensome contribution workflows are adoption problems, and recommends designated responsibility for tags and contributions. The ResearchOps Community likewise describes librarians doing data gardening and developing the research narrative. These sources support operational ownership, rather than expecting storage alone to sustain reuse. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/ · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://researchops.community/blog/project/research-repositories/
- [statement] For research-request intake, Burghardt recommends entry points including intake queues and planning templates, a rubric for self-service versus collaborative support, and explicit communication of contradictions and certainty. Existing research can clarify a request and reveal gaps; analogous findings require judgment rather than being treated as exact answers. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1

## Facts and statements

- [statement] For government user research, the GOV.UK Service Manual says to keep consent records with the research data and make them matchable, and to reuse or share the data only for the purpose covered by that consent. This supports consent-compatible evidence links without assuming repository access grants permission for new uses. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy
- [statement] For research outputs, the Service Manual recommends fully anonymised extracts where possible. If an output is not fully anonymised, restrict access to people who need it and share it only with the third parties disclosed to participants. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy
- [statement] Display research dates and assess applicability before reuse. Burghardt proposes context-sensitive durability rules and review states; these are illustrative governance choices, not validated universal expiry periods. (medium confidence) — https://skimle.com/blog/building-a-research-repository-that-people-actually-use · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] For research-request intake, Burghardt proposes using intake queues and planning entry points to connect questions with existing findings, choosing self-service or researcher support by question importance, query complexity, and research literacy. He recommends making contradictions and uncertainty explicit in the answer. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1
- [statement] NN/g’s repository study used a practitioner survey and follow-up interviews. Its findings describe reported adoption barriers and associations; they should not be treated as an experiment proving that purchasing a repository tool improves decisions. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/
- [statement] Repository rollout advice differs: Zack Naylor, Aurelius co-founder writing for UX Mastery, recommends starting now; NN/g reports that organisations with low UX maturity may lack readiness and stakeholder buy-in. Treat the first position as vendor practitioner advice, not a universal adoption rule. (low confidence) — https://uxmastery.com/how-to-organize-and-reuse-research-insights/ · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-repositories-fail/
- [statement] GOV.UK advises approved storage for research data, restricting access to those who specifically need it, and preventing copying or downloading where technology permits. These recommendations apply to repository source data as well as research outputs that remain identifiable. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/managing-user-research-data-participant-privacy
- [statement] For revalidation, Burghardt proposes stakeholder flags, researcher reviews during reuse, targeted manual review, metadata-based automation and recurring broader review. These are alternative curation approaches with different effort requirements, not evidence that every repository needs an automated expiry policy. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/extending-insight-shelf-life-to-get-more-value-from-research-in-product-planning-c2fb7af5d42a
- [statement] For decision traceability, Burghardt recommends links from planning artifacts to research rationale, recording resulting goals or backlog items, and keeping a register of insight pulls. His reported Amazon experience illustrates how citations connected research to later launches; he explicitly limits that account to one time and context, so it does not establish a general causal effect on business outcomes. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/integrating-research/starting-with-related-research-while-identifying-product-questions-to-get-more-done-with-insights-4789ec7792d1 · keywords: ResearchOps evidence repositories and reuse governance · also: https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions
- [statement] Citation governance should preserve enough context to assess a decision: Burghardt warns that isolated evidence can be cherry-picked, retention-driven deletion can break evidence links, and even citation patterns do not prevent citing the wrong insights. An insight summary can include both supporting and contradicting evidence, but takes additional preparation effort. (low confidence) — https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/citations-are-missing-link-in-insight-driven-decisions
